lead: A semiconductor sensor is a device where the material itself senses. Light, heat, gas, strain or a magnetic field changes the free-carrier density or the width of an internal barrier, and the change appears as a current or voltage. The material choice fixes sensitivity, temperature range and selectivity: silicon for piezoresistors, Hall plates and photodiodes; metal oxides for gases; ceramics and wide-bandgap crystals where silicon would fail.
prereq: You need the piezoresistive effect and semiconductor strain gauges from resistive transducers, the Hall effect and photodiodes from the magnetic and photoelectric transducers, and the p-n junction from basic electronics.

sections.h3: Why a semiconductor is a good transducer

blocks.text: A metal has about 10²⁹ free electrons per m³, fixed. Undoped silicon has about 10¹⁶ per m³ at room temperature; doping raises this to about 10²¹ to 10²³ m⁻³, still far below a metal. Light, heat or an adsorbed molecule can then change the number by a large fraction. That large relative change is why semiconductor sensors exist: the readout circuit can be simple and cheap.

Conductivity is σ = q(nμ<sub>n</sub> + pμ<sub>p</sub>), where σ is in S/m, q = 1.6 × 10<sup>−19</sup> C, n and p are electron and hole densities per m³, and μ<sub>n</sub>, μ<sub>p</sub> are mobilities in m²/(V·s). A sensor disturbs one of these four numbers. Light raises n and p, as in a photoconductor. Strain changes μ by deforming the band structure (it shifts the energy valleys the carriers sit in), which is the piezoresistive effect. A gas changes surface charge and so the depletion width.

The second readout is a barrier: a p-n diode, Schottky diode or MOS capacitor. Its depletion width and built-in voltage Vbi depend on doping, temperature and surface charge, so junction current or capacitance carries the measurement. Solid-electrolyte and surface-acoustic-wave devices are in solid electrolyte and SAW sensors.

In doped silicon at room temperature the carrier density is fixed by the doping, so resistance drifts only about +0.1 to +0.3 %/K, mainly because mobility falls as T rises. The intrinsic carrier density doubles roughly every 10 K, but it overtakes the doping only at high temperature. A piezoresistor bridge therefore needs a constant-current supply or a thermistor correction in the same package.

Silicon is the default: cheap, single-crystal, and micromachined into diaphragms and beams (MEMS micro sensors). Its piezoresistive gauge factor is about 100–200, against about 2 for a metal gauge, because strain changes mobility as well as geometry. Photodiodes respond from 400 nm to 1100 nm, peaking near 850 nm. Plain silicon fails above about 150 °C because junction leakage grows exponentially and the piezoresistor resistance drifts too much for a stable reading; at much higher temperatures the intrinsic carrier density also becomes comparable to the doping.

Silicon carbide (SiC, gap 3.2 eV) and gallium nitride (GaN, gap 3.4 eV) keep both effects small to several hundred degrees Celsius. SiC pressure and gas sensors are quoted for 300–500 °C: engine exhaust, turbine inlets, downhole tools. They cost many times more per wafer, so they appear only where silicon cannot survive.

Metal oxides are the gas and humidity family: SnO₂, ZnO, TiO₂, ZrO₂, Ga₂O₃. Adsorbed oxygen ions take electrons from the surface. An oxidising gas such as oxygen or NO₂ pulls more electrons out and widens the depletion layer, so resistance rises. A reducing gas such as CO or ethanol reacts with the ions, gives the electrons back, and resistance falls. The reaction needs heat, so these sensors run at 200–500 °C from a small heater and draw tens to hundreds of milliwatts. ZrO₂ is the exception: a solid electrolyte oxygen sensor working by Nernst EMF (solid electrolyte and SAW sensors).

GaAs and InP give fast, low-noise and infrared devices: GaAs Hall plates, InGaAs photodiodes for 1300–1550 nm. Conducting polymers such as polypyrrole and polyaniline (PANI) work at room temperature — ammonia and humidity change their doping — but they age and drift. Piezoelectric materials: the ceramic lead zirconate titanate (PZT) and single-crystal quartz convert force to charge. PZT is limited by its Curie point, typically 200–350 °C; quartz is limited by its α–β transition near 573 °C and, in practice, to a few hundred degrees Celsius. Both feed ultrasonic and acoustic sensors and surface acoustic wave devices (solid electrolyte and SAW sensors).

Medicine uses each family. The disposable blood-pressure transducer on an arterial line is a silicon piezoresistive bridge on a diaphragm; a pulse oximeter reads red and infrared light with silicon photodiodes; an ISFET measures blood and gastric pH; and metal-oxide or electrochemical cells monitor anaesthetic and breath gases.

sections.h3: Scaling: why the sensor got small

blocks.text: A surface reaction happens at the surface, but the signal comes from the volume. The figure of merit is surface-to-volume ratio, 6/a for a cube of side a. Going from 1 mm to 1 µm raises it a thousandfold, so a gas sensor becomes faster and more sensitive because most atoms can meet the gas.
One 150 mm wafer holds thousands of dies, so cost per die falls with die area. A mature MEMS pressure sensor die costs a few tens of rupees; packaging is most of the price.

Small is not free. Signal power falls with sensing volume, so 1/f noise and amplifier offset grow relative to the signal. Drift over months — doping change, contamination, package stress — becomes larger than the effect measured. Below a few micrometres, package, drift and noise set accuracy, not the material. Shrink until drift or packaging dominates, then stop. Biosensor versions are in biosensor classes, ISFET, IMFET and glucose sensors.

figure.caption: Left: in clean air adsorbed O⁻ ions trap electrons and leave a thick depleted shell on every grain, so the necks between grains conduct poorly; CO burns off the oxygen and gives the electrons back, so R falls from 60 kΩ to 4 kΩ (S = 15). Right: going from 1 mm to 1 µm raises A/V from 6 × 10³ to 6 × 10⁶ m⁻¹.

examples.question: Compare the surface-to-volume ratio of a 1 mm cube of sensing oxide with a 1 µm cube. How many times larger is the small cube's ratio, and how much more total surface do the small cubes have for the same total volume?
steps: Ratio = 1000. For the same volume, 10⁹ small cubes fit in the large one, so total area is also 1000 times larger.
examples.answer: The 1 µm cube has 1000 times the surface-to-volume ratio and 1000 times the total surface for the same volume.

examples.question: A silicon piezoresistor of 2.0 kΩ with gauge factor 150 is strained by 500 microstrain. Find the resistance change.
steps: New resistance 2150 Ω. A metal gauge (GF = 2) would give 2 Ω.
examples.answer: The piezoresistor changes by 150 Ω, from 2000 Ω to 2150 Ω.
examples.check:
GF = 150
R = 2000.0
eps = 500e-6
dR = GF*eps*R
print(dR)
print(R + dR)

traps: Saying a smaller sensor is always better. Below a few micrometres, packaging, drift and 1/f noise decide accuracy, not the film.
Forgetting the heater. A SnO₂ gas sensor at room temperature gives almost no response; state the 200–500 °C operating temperature.
Calling ZrO₂ a gas-sensitive resistor. It is a solid electrolyte producing a Nernst EMF, a different mechanism needing a reference electrode.
Quoting silicon above 150 °C. There junction leakage and piezoresistor drift spoil the reading; use SiC, GaN or an oxide.

quiz.q: Name four metal oxides used as gas-sensitive resistors and their usual operating temperature.
quiz.a: SnO₂, ZnO, TiO₂ and Ga₂O₃ (ZrO₂ is a solid electrolyte instead). They are heated to about 200–500 °C so the surface reaction is fast.

quiz.q: Why does the resistance of a SnO₂ film fall when carbon monoxide reaches it?
quiz.a: Adsorbed oxygen ions have taken electrons from the SnO₂ film, leaving a depletion layer and high resistance. CO reacts with those ions, forming CO₂, and releases the electrons. Carrier density n rises, σ = q(nμ<sub>n</sub> + pμ<sub>p</sub>) rises, resistance falls.

quiz.q: A silicon piezoresistor of 5.0 kΩ with gauge factor 120 is strained by 200 microstrain. Find the change in resistance.
A cube of sensing oxide has side 0.5 mm. Compute its surface-to-volume ratio and say what side length would give ten times that ratio.
quiz.a: A/V = 6/a = 6/(5 × 10⁻⁴ m) = 1.2 × 10⁴ m⁻¹. Ten times needs a ten times smaller cube: 5 × 10⁻⁵ m = 50 µm, giving 1.2 × 10⁵ m⁻¹.

quiz.q: A designer shrinks a gas-sensing die from 2 mm to 20 µm and finds the response faster but the reading less repeatable month to month. Explain both observations.
quiz.a: The surface-to-volume ratio rises 100 times (6/a), so the gas reaches a larger fraction of the material and the response is faster. The sensing volume falls 10⁶ times; signal power falls while 1/f noise and amplifier offset stay fixed. Contamination and adsorbed species also change a larger fraction of the film. Drift and noise dominate; improve packaging and recalibrate rather than shrink further.

quiz.q: Why is silicon carbide preferred over silicon for a pressure sensor inside a car exhaust pipe, even at ten times the wafer cost?
quiz.a: Above about 150 °C silicon junction leakage grows exponentially and piezoresistor resistance drifts too much for a stable reading; at much higher temperatures the intrinsic carrier density also becomes comparable to the doping. SiC has a 3.2 eV gap, so both effects stay small to several hundred degrees Celsius. Correct operation at 300–500 °C is worth the higher material cost.

beyond: Not for the exam. Research pushes thinner oxide films and nanowires for ppb gas levels, two-dimensional films such as graphene and MoS₂ for room-temperature gas and humidity sensing, and GaN high-electron-mobility structures for harsh environments. Shared multi-project wafer runs let small Indian start-ups and student projects get a few hundred MEMS or ISFET dies cheaply.
